bullets: A line where you stake yourself on a player now counts for far more than a pile of compliments.
How much he buys it depends on his trust in you, the promises you've kept or broken with him, and where he sees himself on the team.
A player who doesn't trust you shrugs off the big line and trusts you a little less.
Saying it again right away adds nothing, and saying it again soon adds little.
Generic praise counts a little each time and stops adding up after three or four lines.
435.look: in a one-on-one with a starter who trusts you, tell him he's your guy once, then compare that with a few rounds of praise.
435.title: Live talks: one strong line against generic praise
435.tldr: When you tell a player he's your guy and mean it, he weighs it like a real commitment. Players who trust you take it to heart, and empty praise stops piling up.

bullets: Typing "you don't have a future here", "you'd play more somewhere else" or "you'll be my last choice" to a backup, a benched starter or a man eyeing the portal now settles his year, the same way the old answer buttons did.
Naming one of his real strengths when you promise him a role makes him believe you more. If you name one that isn't really above his teammates, it sounds like a line.
You can take back a promise, push its date, add a condition, put it in writing or tell him the real reason it hasn't happened, all in your own words.
436.look: a one-on-one with a backup who is thinking about the transfer portal.
436.title: Live talks: your word on his future and promise changes work when typed

bullets: Typing on a contract page calls his agent, and your words go into that call.

bullets: A hot coach's pay is bid up by the schools and clubs that want him, and his own school can counter to keep him.
Winning coaches get raises and early extensions; NFL head coaches sign real deals that owners pay out when they fire them.
NFL owners can fire a head coach in season; a coordinator takes over as interim and may keep the job.
Coordinators and position coaches can be fired during the season at every level, high school included.
A head coach who keeps his job can now clean out as much of his staff as he wants.
438.look: the news during the season and the coaching carousel.

bullets: Every recruit and transfer gets the price that wins him, not a fixed rate for his position.
Schools make offers to keep their starters before the January window.
The biggest programs have real 2026 money, and Group of 5 and FCS schools share revenue by what they can afford.
NIL Go checks deals against what similar players are actually paid.

bullets: Your coaches know the players they coach, so "work with him on his releases" lands on the right man.

467.look: the program grades on the team picker for a team that just went 2-10.
467.title: Playing time grade reads next fall's depth chart
467.tldr: A school's playing time grade now comes from its real depth chart, so a struggling team with weak starters shows the openings recruits expect.

bullets: A 3-4 club and a 4-3 club now see the same edge rusher or tackle differently.
Clubs where the head coach has the final say lean hardest on fit; owners a little less than GMs.
Your own board reads fit too, and "Players who fit what we run" still leans on it more.
468.look: your war room board against the mock drafts, for front-seven players.
468.title: Every club's draft board reads scheme fit
468.tldr: Every NFL club now grades draft prospects for its own scheme, so boards split the way real ones do.

bullets: A player's legs and his upper body are now rated apart: the squat and power clean read the legs, the bench the upper body.
Leg strength drives blocks, bull rushes and runs after contact, and hand strength wins the hand fight and sheds blocks.
College strength programs now show on the bench: a receiver can add a third to his max over four years.
Some players respond to the weight room far better than others, and it shows in their strength and testing numbers.
469.look: your strength coach's testing days over a player's first two college years.
469.title: Progression step 3: upper and lower body strength, the bench at the real slope, the weight room by body knack
469.tldr: Players now have separate upper and lower body strength, and the weight room builds some bodies far more than others.

470.title: Ground: the spec and the round files
470.tldr: The spec for Ground, the offseason game (college), from the Ground list GR1-GR79, every item agreed by Cain 2026-11-06 to 2026-11-15 ("Okay start the build", 2026-11-15 23:47 UTC).

471.title: Ground lane G1a: areas and map data

bullets: Sons and nephews of the world's Pro Bowlers and Hall of Famers come through high school with the family name and its hype.
The commitments of the class's best-known recruits make big news, and the biggest one leads the national news.
Landing a recruit with one of the class's biggest followings lifts your brand exposure for a year.
Recruits with big followings care more about a program's stage.
College players and recruits with huge followings can now land in a social media storm.
472.look: a recruit's family notes for a famous father, and the recruiting news when the class's biggest following commits.
472.title: Ground lane G8: a following and famous names (GR42-GR46)
472.tldr: Famous NFL names now run in families, and a recruit's following matters: the hype kid makes national news, lifts your brand and weighs your stage when he picks.

bullets: A school's name grows each summer with its former players who are in college and the NFL.
Rising schools get more exposure, so their kids get seen and recruited more.
Standouts transfer in to the risers, and families move into the district so their son can play right away where the state allows it.
Each state's transfer rule now decides how many kids move.
The news tells you when a school joins or drops out of its state's powerhouses.
473.look: a high school's page and the June news.
473.title: Ground lane G11a: the high school chain reaction
473.tldr: High schools now rise and fall on their players. A school that sends kids to college and the NFL grows its name, and one that stops producing slowly fades.

bullets: Your evaluation days, calls, camps and campus visits build standing with each kid's coach, his coordinators and his counselor.
When a coach moves up a level he tells you himself, in his own words, after lunch in his planning period.
Ground you stop working fades, and your staff warns you before a level slips, with who was there instead.
Pulling an offer or breaking a promise costs you with his coach for years. His kids starting, graduating and getting drafted with you pays.
Your own high school and hometown know you from day one.
474.look: your inbox after a few spring evaluation weeks.
474.title: Ground lane G1b: standing and one memory
474.tldr: The people around the kids now remember you. Every high school coach and counselor you deal with has a standing with your staff, from Stranger to Home, and it moves with the work you put in.

bullets: Settings has Other versions: every published build with its date and what changed, and an Install button.
Before it installs, AFM tells you which saves a newer build wrote, and keeps a copy of all of them.
While you stay on the older build AFM stops updating itself; Go back to the latest ends that.
475.look: Settings, Other versions (shows up after the next build is out).
475.title: Settings: install an older version and go back to the latest
475.tldr: If a new build is too buggy to play, Settings can now put an older one back, and your saves are copied aside first.

bullets: A Years box sits beside every NIL promise and portal offer, and a Term column is on the NIL desk.
Some players value a guaranteed deal and take less a year for it. Others would rather sign year to year and sell themselves again.
A player who transfers out of a multi-year deal owes half of what's left. The school that takes him pays it to you.
Rival schools now lock up their own blue-chips and top transfers, and renegotiate to keep them.
476.look: your NIL desk's Term column, and the Years box on a five-star's promise.
476.title: NIL lane B: multi-year deals (the new NIL scheme, item 12)
476.tldr: You can now sign recruits, transfers and your own players to NIL deals of up to four years. Locking in a star costs a buyout for anyone who wants to poach him.

477.title: Docs: multi-year deals, five-star money decision (by proxy)

bullets: College and pro strength staffs pick players whose bodies trail their position and put them on a strength program.
A player who takes to it can add a lot of strength and carry more weight. One who doesn't gains almost nothing.
Tall, light frames have the most room to fill. Short, heavy ones have less.
A rebuild costs a little speed for the added pounds and adds some wear.
478.look: a lanky receiver's strength and weight over his college years.
478.title: Progression step 3c: body projects on their leashes, by body knack and frame
478.tldr: Strength staffs can now rebuild a player's body over several years, and some bodies take to it far better than others.

bullets: Asking your athletic director for NIL, staff or recruiting money in your own words is weighed on what you offer in return, your record, their trust in you and the budget, not a fixed answer.
If you put up a bar like a top-3 class or a bowl, a yes makes it a goal your boss holds you to, and the next goals meeting keeps it.
A yes stands for most of a year. Ask again for the same money before then and you'll hear why not.
A no comes with the real reason: the budget, a recent no, a record that doesn't back your promise, or not enough trust yet.
Asking for more time, for your boss to vouch for you with the big booster, or for a booster's money works the same way.
479.look: a sit-down with your athletic director, asking for more NIL money for a top-3 class.
479.title: Weigh a typed ask to your boss or a booster as said, not on the meeting's chip
479.tldr: When you ask your boss or a booster for something in your own words, they now weigh what you actually said and tell you why. Put something on the line, like a top-3 class or nine wins, and see if they buy it.

bullets: A coordinator you inherit fights for his job: he makes his case from his record, asks where he stands and takes bad news his own way.
Everyone knows who you are in the room, so nobody mixes you up with the coach you replaced.
Small talk stays small: ask about the family and he tells you about his family.
An offer gets a real answer before he brings up his own worries.
The talk page now shows what's at stake before you start.
480.look: meet a holdover coordinator in your first week and ask him why you should keep him.
480.title: Live talks: every person plays toward his own goals, and stays on topic
480.tldr: The people you talk to now know what the talk means to them, and they answer what you actually said.

bullets: Every week opens with one line on what matters, taken from the real recruiting calendar.
Your coordinator plans who goes where and why; you can change any man's days or hand the week over.
Road days come off the spring and fall limits as your coaches travel, and your budget decides who flies.
Calls to busy high school coaches leave a message, and they call back in their planning period; your men phone in from the road at night.
The May list arrives the day after Memorial Day, and you can take a week off in July.
481.look: the recruiting desk's Monday digest during the spring evaluation period.
481.title: Ground lane G3: your week and road days
481.tldr: Your recruiting week now has a shape: a Monday letter from your coordinator, your staff out on the road day by day inside the real evaluation limits, and coaches who call you back when they're out of class.

bullets: A recruit's family remembers you for his younger brother, and never forgets a lie.
Word gets around: what you do for one coach's kid reaches his staff and his area.
When a coach moves on, your standing goes with him, and his successor may already know you.
Each person tells you a new level in their own words, and their page shows why you stand where you do.
482.look: a high school coach you visit often, and the family of a recruit you call.
482.title: Ground lane G7: people in full
482.tldr: The people on your recruiting ground now feel like people: coaches, families, counselors, trainers and 7v7 men each remember you, talk to each other and take what you built with them to their next job.

bullets: A new Ground section in the sidebar with The map.
Each recruiting area is shaded by who leads it, with your standing beside it and fog where you haven't worked yet.
Pick an area to see who leads it, where you stand and its head coaches by name.
Open any school for its coaches, where its kids went, its seasons and the players you've signed from it.
483.look: open The map in the Ground section and click your home area.
483.title: Ground lane S1: the map screen and the school page
483.tldr: Ground has a map: see which programs hold each recruiting area in your state, where you stand, and who the people are.

bullets: News about a kid reaches the staffs his coach trusts first, and everyone else later.
High school coaches give you their list, and they tell you more the better they know you.
Each lead shows what you still don't know about the kid, and you can send your staff to fill it in.
Offer a kid the world rates low and he becomes your find. Every step he climbs lifts the coach who told you and your name as a finder.
Your board now shows the kids your own ground found, next to the ones everyone rates.
484.look: your leads list in spring, then a lead's card and its blanks.
484.title: Ground lane G4: news in order, leads, finds and your board from your ground
484.tldr: The ground now feeds your recruiting board. Coaches you know call you first with news and point you to kids nobody rates yet, and the kids you find early pay back when they bloom.

bullets: Saying you're thinking about benching, cutting or moving someone no longer counts as having decided it.
Ask a coach for his read on a player and he tells you where that player stands at his spot, how high he could go, and whether he'd keep him.
If you tell a coach about a cut you've made to someone else, that cut no longer lands on the coach.
Softened announcements like "I think I'm going to have to let you go" still count as decisions.
485.look: sit down with a position coach and ask him to look at one of his players before you decide on a cut.
485.title: Live talks: the ear reads asks and hedges as said, and a coach gives his read on a player
485.tldr: Your staff now hear "take a look at him, I want to decide if we should cut him" as a request for their read, not as a cut, and they answer with what they actually think of the player.

bullets: A new Ground screen, The meeting, with the road days and your free hours for the week.
Each place that wants a man is a numbered stop on the map, with who goes and where you stand there.
Your coordinator puts one call to you each week; make it or leave it to him.
Drag a man to another day to change his road, or hand the whole week to your coordinator.
486.look: open The meeting from the Ground section on a spring Monday.
486.title: Ground lane S2: the meeting at the map
486.tldr: Monday's meeting is a screen: your coordinator's letter, a map of where he wants to send each man, and the week day by day, which you can change by dragging.

bullets: Arm length, hand size and wingspan follow each position's real spread.
Receivers, backs and defensive backs vary in height and weight like real players.
Linemen have a long heavy side, so a few very big men show up.
High school coaches fill their rosters closer to real position shares.
487.look: the measurables on a college player's page.
487.title: Progression step 4a: real body sizes, arms, hands and wingspans, and placement's fractional need
487.tldr: Players now come in the real range of body shapes for their position, so you'll find short-armed tackles, long-armed corners, light receivers and the occasional huge guard.

488.title: Ground lane G11b: favors, switched off

bullets: Open a coach from the map or a school to see his memory of you, dated, newest first.
See your staff's read of how good and how straight he is, and what kind of man he is.
See what Known gets you with him, and what Trusted would.
See where he stands with every other staff, and who he is tied to.
The new People page lists everyone you have dealt with.
489.look: pick a coach on the map's "Who matters here" list.
489.title: Ground lane S5: the person screen
489.tldr: Every coach, trainer and family on your ground now has a page: his face, what he keeps of you in his own words, and what your standing gets you.

bullets: The vertical and broad jump spread like real ones, and strong legs help.
Quarterbacks and backs no longer broad jump like receivers.
The very fastest 3-cones and shuttles are rare, as they are in real life.
Drill results are no longer capped, so a record-breaking day prints as it happened.
490.title: Progression step 4b: drills on real, a jump knack, thin fast 3-cone and shuttle, no printed limits
490.tldr: Combine numbers now look like a real combine: real jump averages by position, the odd explosive leaper, and agility records that are hard to touch.

bullets: Talk your AD's goals down, take them bigger or ask why, and pick your own from a list of 63.
Every Monday you can change your own goal, and your coordinator warns you when one slips.
Long shots pay the most when you make them; sure things cost the most when you miss.
In your first offseason your coordinator walks you through your ground, three schools at a time, until you send him off.
After the verdict, a ground report sums up the spring: your goals, finds, areas and who outworked you.
493.look: your coordinator's February meeting memo and the AD's office the day after signing day.
493.title: Ground lane G6: the offseason campaign
493.tldr: Your first college spring now has a shape: your AD sets his goals for the class the day after signing day, your coordinator brings his at the February meeting, and the verdict comes the week before your first game.
